nameStory: The Pacific Loon gets its name from its primary breeding grounds around the northern Pacific Ocean, including Alaska and western Canada. Though called 'Pacific,' these wandering water birds occasionally show up along New England's Atlantic coast during migration and winter, much to the delight of birdwatchers who consider them a special treat.
description: The Pacific Loon is a sleek, medium-sized water bird that's built like a living torpedo for diving after fish. It's smaller than the familiar Common Loon but larger than the petite Red-throated Loon, with a streamlined body perfectly designed for underwater hunting. These elegant birds have a distinctive straight, pointed bill and sit low in the water with their bodies partially submerged, making them look like they're always ready to disappear beneath the surface.

idTips.label: Bill shape and angle
idTips.description: The bill appears perfectly straight and dagger-like when viewed from the side, held level with the head rather than angled upward like other loons

idTips.label: Head shape
idTips.description: The head has a smoothly rounded, almost snake-like profile that flows seamlessly into the neck without the blocky appearance of Common Loons

idTips.label: Size and posture
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than Common Loons but larger than Red-throated Loons, sitting very low in the water with only the neck and head clearly visible above the surface

idTips.label: Winter plumage pattern
idTips.description: Shows a clean contrast between dark gray back and bright white underparts, with a thin dark strap across the back of the neck

idTips.label: Flight silhouette
idTips.description: Flies with rapid wingbeats close to the water surface, showing a hunchbacked profile with the neck extended straight forward and feet trailing behind

habitat: Pacific Loons are most likely spotted in New England's coastal waters, including protected bays, harbors, and nearshore ocean areas during migration and winter months. They prefer deeper waters where they can dive for fish, often seen from rocky headlands, piers, or beaches along the Atlantic coast. Unlike Common Loons, they rarely venture onto inland lakes and ponds during their brief visits to our region.

seasonality.spring: Rare migrants may pass through coastal waters in April and May, usually in basic (non-breeding) plumage as they head north to Arctic breeding grounds.
seasonality.summer: Extremely rare in New England during summer months, as adults are busy nesting on remote tundra lakes in Alaska and northwestern Canada.
seasonality.fall: Best chance for sightings occurs from October through December when birds migrate south along the coast, occasionally stopping to rest and feed in sheltered bays.
seasonality.winter: Small numbers may linger in ice-free coastal waters through winter, particularly during mild years when harbors and bays remain open.

funFact: Pacific Loons can dive to depths of over 200 feet and stay underwater for more than two minutes, using their wings like flippers to 'fly' through the water while chasing fish - they're essentially aerial acrobats that happen to perform their best tricks underwater!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Red-throated Loon in winter plumage, but Pacific Loon's straight bill (versus Red-throated's upturned bill) and smoother head profile are key differences. Remember: 'Pacific = perfect posture' - the bill stays level and straight, while Red-throated Loons tilt their bills upward like they're snobbishly looking down their nose at you.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Pacific' Loons, these birds actually breed across the Arctic tundra from Alaska to Hudson Bay, making their name somewhat misleading. The 44 recorded sightings in New England represent genuine rarities that generate excitement among local birders, as each appearance is unpredictable and special.
compareHints: Pacific Loons are the 'Goldilocks' of their family - not as large and blocky as Common Loons, not as small and delicate as Red-throated Loons, but just right in between. Their perfectly straight bill sets them apart from both relatives, while their clean winter plumage lacks the speckled back pattern often seen on Red-throated Loons. Think of them as the sleekest, most streamlined member of the loon family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common loons are much larger than red-throated loons, their only regular loon relative in New England waters.
Red-throated loons are much smaller and more delicate-looking than Common Loons, with a thinner neck and that characteristic upward-tilted bill.
Yellow-billed Loons dwarf their Common Loon cousins in size and have that unmistakable straight yellow bill versus the Common Loon's dark, slightly curved bill.
